content: The carat is a unit of mass specifically used for measuring gemstones and pearls. It is equivalent to 200 milligrams (0.2 grams) or approximately 3.086 grains. This standardized definition, known as the metric carat, was officially adopted in 1907 during the Fourth General Conference on Weights and Measures and was subsequently implemented in many countries worldwide. Today, the metric carat is universally recognized and used. The carat is further subdivided into 100 points, with each point representing 2 milligrams. In the context of diamonds, a paragon refers to a flawless stone weighing at least 100 carats (20 grams). The standard abbreviation for carat in the 12 EDI system is CD. The term carat has its etymological roots in the Greek word kerátion (κεράτιον), meaning fruit of the carob, which was adopted into Arabic as qīrāṭ (قيراط) and later into Italian as carato before entering the English language. The Latin equivalent of carat is siliqua. Historically, different countries had their own carat units, which were approximately equivalent to the weight of a carob seed. These units were often used for weighing gold. Carob seeds were historically employed as weights on precision scales due to their perceived uniformity in mass. However, a 2006 study revealed that carob seeds exhibit as much variation in weight as other seeds. Despite this, carob seeds were easier to standardize by identifying and removing outliers, which made them suitable for use as a weight standard. Historical Definitions in the United Kingdom Board of Trade Carat In the United Kingdom, prior to 1888, the Board of Trade carat was defined as exactly 3 1647/9691 grains. After 1887, it was redefined as exactly 3 17/101 grains. Although it was a non-metric unit, several metric countries adopted this unit for its limited applications. The Board of Trade carat was divisible into four diamond grains, but measurements were typically made in multiples of 1/64 carat. Unlike the modern carat, the Board of Trade carat was not used for measuring pearls, which were instead measured using pearl grains. Pound Carat and Ounce Carat Two additional varieties of refiners' carats were once used in the United Kingdom: the pound carat and the ounce carat. The troy pound was divided into 24 pound carats, each weighing 240 troy grains. Each pound carat was further divided into four pound grains of 60 troy grains each, and each pound grain was subdivided into four pound quarters of 15 troy grains each. Similarly, the troy ounce was divided into 24 ounce carats, each weighing 20 troy grains. Each ounce carat was divided into four ounce grains of 5 troy grains each, and each ounce grain was subdivided into four ounce quarters of 1.25 troy grains. The Carat of the Romans and Greeks The solidus (carat) was also a Roman unit of weight. Historical evidence suggests that the weight of 72 coins of the type called solidus equaled one Roman pound, and the weight of a single solidus was 24 siliquae. This corresponds to approximately 4.5 grams, or possibly up to 5 grams less. Therefore, the metric equivalent of one solidus was approximately 189 milligrams. The Greeks had a similar unit of the same value. The Carat in Byzantine Egypt In Byzantine and early Arab periods, a carob-based weight unit was used in Egypt. Glass weights were employed for weighing coins, and from these, the weight of the Egyptian carat has been reconstructed as approximately 196 milligrams. This aligns with the average weight of carob seeds in the region. The Syrian and Arabic Carat in Mohammad's Time Literary sources indicate that the Arabic carat was only 2% lighter than the Syrian carat. Based on coins and glass weights, their weight has been reconstructed as approximately 212 milligrams. This is consistent with historical accounts that a solidus weighed slightly less than 22 carats. Notes 1. The United States adopted the metric carat definition on July 1, 1913, and the United Kingdom followed on April 1, 1914. 2. The literal translation of the Greek word kerátion is little horn, which describes the shape of the carob seed pod. 3. A 2006 study by Turnbull et al. in New Scientist found that carob seeds have weight variations similar to other seeds, but their standardization was easier due to the ability to identify and remove outliers. 4. Refiners' carats originated as a measure of gold fineness. 5. Historical references include works by William Chaffers (1883) and Philip Grierson (1960).
